Filings we handle

Income tax, GST and ROC filings. Select any service and it is filled into the enquiry form for you.

ITR-1 filing

Sahaj. The simple return for resident individuals with salary, pension, house property or interest income.

Who can file
Resident individuals with total income up to ₹50 lakh, no business income, foreign assets or unlisted shares.
Due date
31 July.
If missed
Late fee up to ₹5,000 and 1% monthly interest on unpaid tax.
Enquire

ITR-2 filing

For individuals and HUFs who have capital gains, foreign assets or higher income, but no business income.

Who can file
Individuals and HUFs without business income, who sold shares or property, hold foreign assets, are company directors, or earn above ₹50 lakh.
Due date
31 July.
If missed
Late fee, interest, and capital losses cannot be carried forward.
Enquire

ITR-3 filing

For individuals and HUFs with business or professional income, including traders and partners in a firm.

Who can file
Proprietors, professionals, F&O traders and partners whose income does not fit the presumptive scheme.
Due date
31 August; 31 October where a tax audit applies.
If missed
Late fee, interest, no carry-forward of business losses, and audit default penalty up to ₹1.5 lakh.
Enquire

ITR-4 filing

Sugam. A simpler return for small businesses and professionals who opt for presumptive taxation.

Who can file
Resident individuals, HUFs and firms (not LLPs) under sections 44AD, 44ADA or 44AE, with total income up to ₹50 lakh.
Due date
31 August.
If missed
Late fee up to ₹5,000 and interest on unpaid tax.
Enquire

ITR-5 filing

For partnership firms, LLPs and other associations of persons.

Who can file
Partnership firms, LLPs, AOPs, BOIs and similar bodies. Not for companies, individuals or HUFs.
Due date
31 October where audit applies; otherwise the date notified for the year.
If missed
Late fee up to ₹5,000, interest, lost loss carry-forward and audit default penalty.
Enquire

ITR-6 filing

For companies, prepared from the audited financial statements and tax computation.

Who can file
All companies, except those claiming exemption under section 11 for charitable or religious purposes.
Due date
31 October.
If missed
Late fee up to ₹5,000, interest, lost loss carry-forward, and possible penalties.
Enquire

ITR-7 filing

For trusts, charitable and religious institutions, political parties and similar bodies.

Who can file
Entities that must file under sections 139(4A) to 139(4F), such as charitable trusts, institutions, political parties and business trusts.
Due date
31 October where audit applies; otherwise the date notified for the year.
If missed
Late fee, penalties, and the tax exemption on income can be put at risk.
Enquire

Income tax notice reply

Review of an income tax notice or intimation, with documents and a drafted reply filed on the portal.

Who can file
Anyone who has received a notice, intimation or demand from the income tax department.
Due date
Within the time stated on the notice, often 15 to 30 days.
If missed
Ex-parte assessment on the department's estimate, a demand with interest, and penalties.

Revised return

Corrects mistakes or omissions in a return you have already filed.

Who can file
Taxpayers who filed a return and then found an error, a missed income or deduction, or got new information.
Due date
Generally by 31 December of the assessment year (check the date for your year).
If missed
You can only file an updated return (ITR-U) with additional tax, and it cannot claim a refund.

Common questions

Can you also set up my company, LLP or firm?

Yes. We help you choose the right structure, prepare the documents, complete the registration, and then continue with GST, accounts and annual filings so everything stays with one team.

Do I need GST registration?

It depends on your turnover, what you supply and where you sell. Some businesses must register from the first sale. We will assess your case and handle the application if you need it.

My records are incomplete. Can you still help?

Yes. Send bills, bank statements and whatever you have. We will build the accounts from the available records and set up a simple routine for keeping them current.

Can you handle an income tax or GST notice?

Yes. Send the notice as soon as you receive it. We will explain what it means, prepare the reply and submit it before the deadline.

Do we have to meet in person?

Not necessarily. We value your time, so we do not ask you to travel unless it is really needed. You can share documents online and we will speak by phone or video call. If something still needs a face-to-face discussion, we will meet you at a time that suits you.

How do you charge?

A fixed monthly fee for ongoing compliance, or a one-time fee for registrations and individual returns. You receive the quote before we begin.

The Code on Social Security, 2020 is in force: what it changes for PF, ESI and payroll

The Code replaced the old EPF and ESI Acts and several other social security laws. Contribution rates largely carry over, but the wage definition and the rule books are new.

By KS Financials · Updated 18 Nov 2026 · 4 min read

India's four labour codes were brought into force on 21 November 2025, and the Code on Social Security, 2020 is the one that matters most for payroll. It gathers the Employees' Provident Funds Act, the ESI Act and other older social security laws into a single statute. A year on, the rules and schemes under it have been notified, so employers are now working with the new framework rather than waiting for it.

Please note: the details below come from professional explainers and law-firm updates that we have read against each other, not from a line-by-line reading of the Gazette. Check any figure against the official notification before you apply it.

How the framework came together

DateWhat happened
21 Nov 2025The Code on Social Security, 2020 comes into force, along with the other three labour codes.
8 May 2026Final rules under the Code are reported as notified.
29 May 2026The EPF wage ceiling is notified at ₹15,000 a month, along with other operating parameters such as interest on late contributions.
29 Jun 2026The EPF, Pension (EPS) and Deposit-Linked Insurance (EDLI) Schemes, 2026 are notified and replace the older schemes.
17 Sep 2026The EPF wage ceiling is raised to ₹25,000 a month.

The last three steps each have their own article on this blog. This one explains the foundations.

What stays the same

The basic shape of provident fund contributions carries over. Reports on the 2026 schemes describe the 12% contribution structure as retained, with the changes aimed at administration, withdrawals and compliance. Payroll teams do not need to rebuild the whole salary structure, but they do need to check how "wages" is measured.

The new wage definition and the 50% rule

Under the Code, "wages" is built from basic pay, dearness allowance and retaining allowance. Other components, such as house rent allowance, conveyance and similar allowances, can be left out of wages, but only up to a limit. If the excluded items come to more than half of total remuneration, the excess is added back to wages.

A simple illustration of how the rule works: an employee's total monthly remuneration is ₹40,000, made up of ₹14,000 basic pay and ₹26,000 in allowances. Half of the total is ₹20,000, so allowances of ₹26,000 exceed the limit by ₹6,000. That ₹6,000 is added back, and wages for the Code's purposes become ₹20,000 rather than ₹14,000.

This matters most where a salary has been split into a low basic and large allowances to keep the PF base small. Explainers on the September 2026 notification confirm that the wage definition and the 50% rule were not changed by it.

Wider coverage and other changes reported

  • The Code extends social security towards gig and platform workers and fixed-term employees, with a separate fund for gig and platform workers.
  • ESI coverage is described as no longer limited to notified areas.
  • The deposit required to file an appeal in PF matters is reported as reduced.

Exact applicability for a given establishment depends on its size, activity and state, so confirm it for each client before relying on these points.

What employers should do now

  1. Re-test the wage base. Run each salary structure against the 50% rule and note where wages for PF purposes are higher than the old "basic" figure.
  2. Update payroll references. Statutory labels in payroll software, offer letters and policies should refer to the Code and the 2026 schemes rather than the 1952 Act and scheme.
  3. Check coverage. Look at headcount, contract and fixed-term staff, and whether ESI now reaches your location.
  4. Keep a record. File the notifications you relied on and the reasoning behind your wage calculation, in case of an inspection or query.

If you would like your payroll structure checked against the new wage definition, or help with PF and ESI filings, speak to our team.

Sources

  • Compliance Age: EPF wage ceiling, interest rate and inspection charges notified under the Code
  • LexComply: EPF wage ceiling 2026, wages definition and the 50% proviso
  • Lawrbit: EPF, EPS and EDLI Schemes 2026
  • KPMG: Operationalisation of the special schemes under the Code
  • CrackTarget: Code on Social Security vs old EPF and ESI Acts (secondary source for the coverage points)

This article is general information as at 18 Nov 2026 and is not legal or tax advice for your specific case. Notifications and EPFO circulars change often, so check the current official text before you act.

← All articles EPF wage ceiling

EPF wage ceiling raised to ₹25,000: who is newly covered, and why the pension limit stays at ₹15,000

From 17 September 2026 the PF wage ceiling is ₹25,000 a month. A second notification keeps the Central Government's pension contribution on wages up to ₹15,000, so the two limits must be set up separately in payroll.

By KS Financials · Updated 18 Nov 2026 · 4 min read

For years the EPF wage ceiling stood at ₹15,000 a month. After the Code on Social Security came in, the ceiling was first notified at the same ₹15,000 on 29 May 2026, which gave employers certainty that nothing had changed. Then, on 17 September 2026, the Ministry of Labour and Employment notified a new ceiling of ₹25,000 a month for Chapter III of the Code (the provident fund chapter), replacing the May notification except for things already done under it.

A month later, a second notification dated 15 October 2026 amended the Employees' Pension Scheme, 2026 to say that the Central Government's contribution is limited to wages up to ₹15,000 a month. It took effect from 17 September 2026 as well. The two figures are not contradictory, because they apply to different things.

Please note: the worked figures below come from a professional commentary on the two notifications, not from EPFO's own calculation sheets. Confirm contribution amounts against EPFO circulars and your payroll software before you change any deductions.

The two limits side by side

S.O. 5109(E)G.S.R. 890(E)
Date17 Sep 202615 Oct 2026 (effective 17 Sep 2026)
What it coversWage ceiling for Chapter III (provident fund)Amendment to the Employees' Pension Scheme, 2026
Limit₹25,000 a month₹15,000 a month, for the Central Government contribution

Who is affected

  • Employees earning ₹15,001 to ₹25,000 who were not PF members. They now fall within mandatory coverage, subject to the other conditions of the Code. Employers should generate or link a UAN and start contributions from 17 September 2026.
  • Existing members earning above ₹15,000 whose contributions were limited to ₹15,000. The permitted wage cap for contributions rises to ₹25,000, so employers should review whether to move these employees to the higher base. The month of September will need a pro-rata approach.
  • Employees above ₹25,000. The ceiling does not itself settle their position, so check their membership status and the scheme provisions.

One payroll adviser also notes that pension membership for new joiners is available only where wages are within ₹25,000 at the time of joining. Treat this as a point to confirm with the scheme text.

Why the pension limit stays at ₹15,000

A higher provident fund ceiling does not automatically raise the base on which the Central Government's pension contribution is worked out. The second notification makes ₹15,000 explicit for that contribution. The commentary we have read warns against treating either figure as a single limit for everything.

Monthly wagesEmployee 12%Employer pension (8.33%)Employer PF accountCentral Govt (1.16%, on wages up to ₹15,000)
₹12,000₹1,440₹1,000₹440₹139
₹18,000₹2,160₹1,499₹661₹174
₹25,000₹3,000₹2,083₹917₹174

These are the commentator's illustrations, not a full contribution calculation. They show the point that the Central Government's share stops growing at ₹15,000 even when wages go higher.

What employers should do now

  1. Map the two limits separately in payroll. Do not replace every ₹15,000 with ₹25,000.
  2. List newly covered employees. Anyone earning between ₹15,001 and ₹25,000 who is not yet enrolled needs a UAN and a start date of 17 September 2026.
  3. Decide on the contribution base for existing staff. Where employees were capped at ₹15,000, decide and record whether contributions move to the higher base, and tell staff because take-home pay will fall.
  4. Fix the September arrears. The ceiling applied from the middle of the month, so work out the pro-rata contribution and correct the ECR if needed.
  5. Keep the notifications on file with a short note on how you read them.

If your payroll or ECR needs reviewing after this change, speak to our team.

Sources

  • TaxGuru: EPF wage ceiling ₹25,000 vs EPS ₹15,000, the two notifications
  • SGCMS: EPFO wage ceiling increased from ₹15,000 to ₹25,000, impact on employers
  • Maheshwari & Co: Centre notifies ₹25,000 wage ceiling under the Code
  • KS&K: ₹15,000 wage ceiling notified on 29 May 2026

EPF Scheme, 2026: simpler withdrawals, new compliance rules and the one-time amnesty windows

The 1952 provident fund scheme has been replaced. Members get fewer withdrawal categories, and employers get new compliance duties plus three time-bound schemes to clear old defaults.

By KS Financials · Updated 18 Nov 2026 · 4 min read

On 29 June 2026 the Ministry of Labour and Employment notified the Employees' Provident Funds Scheme, 2026, along with new Pension and Deposit-Linked Insurance schemes. They replace the 1952, 1995 and 1976 schemes and are made under the Code on Social Security, 2020. Existing members move to the new scheme automatically, with no fresh enrolment needed.

Please note: the scheme was reported in many explainers that differ in detail. One summary gives the effective date as the date of publication, 29 June 2026, while another says 1 July 2026. Verify dates, limits and deadlines against the Gazette text and EPFO circulars.

What changes for members

  • Fewer withdrawal heads. The earlier 13 categories of advance withdrawal are regrouped into three: essential needs, housing needs and specified special circumstances.
  • A longer wait for final settlement after job loss. Reports say members will generally have to stay unemployed for 12 months before taking a premature final settlement of the account. Check the scheme paragraph for any exceptions before advising a client.
  • More digital processing. Claims and verification lean further on digital processes.
  • Tax treatment unchanged. The existing income tax rules on EPF contributions and withdrawals are reported as continuing as before.

What changes for employers

The scheme brings updated definitions and new compliance and filing requirements, and it changes how exempted establishments and private PF trusts are treated. It also keeps contribution calculations tied to "wages" as defined in the Code, which we explain in our article on the Code on Social Security.

Three time-bound schemes for past defaults

SchemeWhat it is for
Employees' Enrolment Campaign, 2026Lets employers enrol workers who were missed in the past. It was reported as valid until 31 October 2026, so check whether it has closed or been extended.
VISHWAS, 2026A way to settle damages for defaults in paying contributions that relate to periods before 14 June 2024.
AMNESTY, 2026Lets exempted establishments and PF trusts that operate without a formal exemption regularise their position, on prescribed conditions.

The terms of each scheme, such as the payments due and the last dates, are set in the notification and EPFO's operating circulars. Because these windows are limited, an employer with old defaults should find out now whether it is still eligible.

What to do now

  1. Review your history. Check for missed enrolments, late payments and mismatched wages, particularly for periods before June 2024.
  2. Check each special scheme. Confirm which of the three apply and whether the window is still open.
  3. Brief your staff. Tell employees about the new withdrawal groups and the longer wait after leaving a job, so they plan their claims properly.
  4. Update your processes. Align your monthly ECR, UAN records and claim handling with the new scheme text.

If you need help reviewing old defaults or filing under the new scheme, speak to our team.

Sources

  • EY: New Employees' Provident Funds Scheme and Amnesty 2026 notified
  • KPMG: Operationalisation of the special schemes
  • Mondaq: EPF Scheme 2026, key considerations for private employers
  • Business Standard: EPF withdrawal rules under the new Scheme 2026
  • Lexplosion: EPF Scheme 2026 notified, with VISHWAS and AMNESTY
  • India Briefing: Employee Provident Fund 2026, compliance rules for employers

57th GST Council: arrest powers to go, prosecution limit up to ₹5 crore

The Council's 8 October 2026 meeting recommended the biggest softening of GST enforcement since the law began. Here is what was recommended, what still needs to become law, and what to do now.

By KS Financials · Updated 18 Nov 2026 · 4 min read

The 57th GST Council met in New Delhi on 8 October 2026 under Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman. Most of the attention has gone to enforcement. The Council recommended withdrawing the power to arrest for GST offences, raising the prosecution threshold, and cutting several penalties that small businesses find hardest to bear.

One point matters before everything else: these are recommendations. The Government's own release says they take effect only through circulars, notifications, rule changes or amendments to the CGST and IGST Acts. Until Parliament and the States pass the amendments, the existing provisions stay in force.

1. Arrest powers withdrawn

The Council recommended omitting Section 69 of the CGST Act, which is the section that lets officers arrest a person for specified GST offences. If the amendment is passed, officers would no longer be able to arrest for GST offences at all. Prosecution in court would remain possible for the offences that stay on the statute book.

2. Prosecution threshold raised from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore

Prosecution would begin only where the tax involved crosses ₹5 crore. The Council also recommended narrowing Section 132(1), the list of punishable offences:

  • Clause (c), on wrongly availed input tax credit, would cover only fraudulent claims made without receiving the goods or services, or without an invoice or bill.
  • Clause (i) would be omitted, and the words "evades tax" would be removed from clause (e).
  • The catch-all words "or in any other manner deals with" in clause (h) would be deleted.
  • Punishments would be rationalised. One reading of the proposal is up to 5 years where the amount is above ₹10 crore and up to 2 years for ₹5 to 10 crore, with the six-month minimum removed. This detail comes from a professional commentary rather than the Government release, so wait for the final text.

3. Notices, penalties and appeals

  • No small notices. No show cause notice under Section 73, 74 or 74A where the total tax (CGST, SGST, IGST and cess) is below ₹10,000. The Council said this should also apply to pending notices and appeals.
  • General penalty cut. The maximum under Section 125 drops from ₹25,000 to ₹10,000.
  • 5% penalty for quick payment. In non-fraud cases, the penalty falls to 5% if tax and interest are paid within 30 days of the order (Section 73) or 60 days (Section 74A). The ₹10,000 minimum penalty in non-fraud cases would be removed.
  • Voluntary payment. Where tax, interest and penalty are all paid voluntarily within the time allowed, the penalty would be treated as a charge rather than a punishment.
  • Pre-deposit cap. For appeals against penalty-only orders, the pre-deposit would be capped at ₹40 crore (₹20 crore CGST and ₹20 crore SGST).
  • Better notices. CBIC is to issue a circular on the quality and timing of notices, on invoking fraud or suppression only where the facts justify it, and on personal hearings. A validation clause is also proposed for notices that courts struck down because they covered several financial years.

4. Movement of goods

Sections 68, 129 and 130 would be amended so that trucks are intercepted only on specific intelligence, and only with approval from an officer not below Joint Commissioner. Inspection, detention or seizure would be allowed only where the supplier or recipient is registered in the intercepting State, so no interception by transit States. If there is no e-way bill, or the documents do not show origin or destination, action would be allowed regardless of State. Confiscation under Section 130 would not apply to goods and vehicles in transit.

Does this apply to old cases?

This is not settled. The ₹10,000 notice floor was expressly extended to pending notices and appeals. For the prosecution threshold and the omitted offences, commentators note that the answer will depend on the transitional wording of the amending law and on how courts apply Section 6 of the General Clauses Act. Anyone with a pending prosecution or arrest-related matter should take specific advice and not assume the benefit.

What business owners should do now

  1. Do not relax compliance. Tax, interest and penalties remain payable. The reforms change consequences, not the obligation to file and pay correctly.
  2. Review open notices. List every notice and appeal with the tax amount. Any below ₹10,000 may fall away once the amendment is notified.
  3. Keep the 30 and 60 day windows in mind. If an order is passed and the demand is correct, paying within the window may cut the penalty to 5%.
  4. Keep documents ready. Fraud allegations will still turn on invoices, e-way bills and proof of receipt of goods. Good records protect you under both the old and the new rules.
  5. Watch for the Bill. At the time of writing no date has been announced for the amending Bill. The Winter Session is a possibility, but that is speculation until the Government confirms.

If you have received a GST notice, or want your credit and invoice position reviewed before any change takes effect, our team can help.

Sources

  • Recommendations of the 57th Meeting of the GST Council (PIB)
  • TaxGuru: 57th GST Council's arrest and prosecution reforms and pending cases
  • TaxSlabs: 57th GST Council meeting guide

57th GST Council: what changes for ITC, refunds, registration and returns

Beyond enforcement, the 8 October 2026 meeting recommended easier registration, faster refunds, wider input tax credit and a new return-correction system. These are the points that matter for day-to-day filing.

By KS Financials · Updated 18 Nov 2026 · 4 min read

The 57th GST Council's recommendations on the working side of GST are as significant as the enforcement changes. They aim to cut disputes by fixing problems at the return stage, speed up refunds and make registration less document-heavy. As with every Council meeting, these are recommendations that become binding only through notifications, rule amendments or law changes.

Input tax credit (ITC)

  • Section 17(5) relaxed. The Council recommended removing the credit block for outdoor catering, health and life insurance, telecom towers, pipelines laid outside factory premises, free samples, and goods destroyed or written off on expiry of shelf life where the law requires it. The list was described as not exhaustive.
  • Limited credit in the same line of business. Restaurant and outdoor catering, hotel accommodation up to ₹7,500 per unit per day, and gym and fitness services would get limited credit where the business supplies the same type of service.
  • Rule 86A. When an officer blocks your electronic credit ledger, you would be allowed to object and ask for a personal hearing before the officer decides.

Refunds

  • Automation in two phases. In phase 1, excess balance in the cash ledger would be refunded automatically in full. The acknowledgement or deficiency memo period falls from 15 to 10 days, with deemed acknowledgement if the department does not respond. For zero-rated and inverted-duty claims, 90% would be sanctioned provisionally by the system based on risk. Phase 2 adds system acknowledgement after verification and automatic full sanction for zero-rated supplies, after adjusting any dues.
  • Simpler RFD-01. A system-readable form without scanned uploads for zero-rated and inverted-duty claims.
  • Export refund cap removed. The Rule 89(4)(C) cap that limited zero-rated goods turnover to 1.5 times the value of like goods supplied domestically would go.
  • Inverted duty on services and capital goods. Credit on input services availed on or after 1 November 2026 would become refundable for inverted-duty claims. Credit on capital goods availed on or after 1 April 2027 would also become refundable, spread over 60 months.

As of today the 1 November 2026 date has passed, but a recommendation does not become effective until it is notified, so check the notification before filing a claim on this basis.

Registration

  • A comprehensive circular and FAQs listing the documents needed, with drop-down options in REG-01 and a more guided portal. The aim is fewer rejections and fewer queries.
  • Changes to registration particulars would be accepted automatically, except a change of principal place of business for ordinary registrants.
  • Cancellation on the taxpayer's own application would become automatic in phases once returns are filed and dues are paid.
  • System-based cancellation and revocation would be used for non-filing of returns or missing bank details, with a window to fix the default.
  • New Rule 14B. Small e-commerce sellers could register in a State where they have no premises, by declaring the operator's warehouse as their principal place of business. This is automatic where ITC passed on does not exceed ₹2.5 lakh a month.

This builds on the simplified registration route for low-risk applicants, who pass on up to ₹2.5 lakh of ITC a month, under Rule 14A.

Returns and reconciliation

The Council recommended a return-correction framework proposed to apply from the April 2027 return period, after a public consultation. The pieces are:

  • Better matching of GSTR-1, GSTR-1A and the IFF with GSTR-3B.
  • Corrections so that GSTR-3B liability matches GSTR-1 and ITC matches GSTR-2B (new Rules 61(1A) and 61(1B)).
  • Electronic statements for tax paid under reverse charge and ITC claimed (Rule 86D), and for credit reversed and reclaimed (Rule 86C).
  • Statutory backing for the Invoice Management System, including a time limit for pending credit notes.
  • DRC-03 payments to carry the underlying invoice details.

Late fee relief. For taxpayers with previous-year turnover up to ₹5 crore, the late fee on a delayed GSTR-3B under Section 39(1) would be waived if the return is filed by the end of the due month. E-invoicing would extend, for turnover of ₹5 crore and above, to reverse-charge purchases from unregistered persons and to import of services. An optional annual return, quarterly payment scheme for B2C-only suppliers up to ₹5 crore was approved in principle as a concept note and is not yet operational.

Practical steps

  1. Clean up your GSTR-2B reconciliation every month. The correction system will make mismatches visible and harder to ignore.
  2. If you are an exporter or have inverted duty, list your unutilised credit by type (goods, services, capital goods) so you can plan refund claims once notified.
  3. Check whether any credit you have been reversing under Section 17(5) may become claimable, and keep the workings, but do not claim until the change is notified.
  4. Sellers on online marketplaces should look at whether Rule 14B suits them once it is operational.

Sources

  • Recommendations of the 57th Meeting of the GST Council (PIB)

  • TaxGuru: GST Council 57th meeting, arrest powers, ITC, refund and registration reforms
  • CA Rajput: Revamped GST registration scheme

GST 2.0 more than a year on: two slabs, 40% for sin goods and recent rate tweaks

In September 2025 the Council replaced four GST slabs with two main rates. We recap what changed, and the smaller rate decisions that followed in October 2026.

By KS Financials · Updated 18 Nov 2026 · 3 min read

At its 56th meeting on 3 September 2025, the GST Council approved the most visible change to GST rates since 2017. The old structure of 5%, 12%, 18% and 28% was replaced by two main rates, 5% and 18%, with a special 40% rate for a short list of luxury and sin goods. The new rates came into effect on 22 September 2025. Because this change touched almost every invoice, it is worth revisiting what it meant and what has been added since.

The structure in brief

  • 5% for most essential and everyday goods and services. Many items that earlier carried 12% moved here, including a range of textiles, fertilisers, renewable energy equipment and agriculture-related inputs.
  • 18% as the standard rate. Electronics and white goods such as air conditioners, televisions, refrigerators and washing machines, and small cars, moved down from 28% to 18%.
  • 40% for select luxury and demerit goods, such as tobacco products, private aircraft and yachts. Where compensation cess obligations continue, those goods stay at their existing effective rate until the obligations end.
  • Insurance. Individual health and life insurance premiums were taken from 18% to nil. Group and other policies are treated differently, so check the notification for the specific product.

The headline benefit to consumers is lower prices on many items. For businesses the effect is more mixed, and this is where most of the work landed.

What it meant for businesses

  1. Billing systems. Every rate master, HSN mapping and invoice template had to be updated. Goods billed before 22 September 2025 but supplied after it were the classic trouble spot.
  2. Inverted duty. Where the rate on inputs is higher than the rate on the output, credit builds up. Cutting a 12% product to 5% while its inputs stay at 18% creates exactly this, so refund claims and credit planning matter more.
  3. Stock and pricing. Businesses holding stock bought at the old rate and selling at the new one had to look at margins and price lists.
  4. Classification disputes. A rate gap between two headings invites arguments about which heading a product belongs in. Keep the product description, specification and a note of why you chose the classification.

Rate decisions at the 57th meeting (8 October 2026)

The 57th Council did not redraw the slabs, but it recommended several rate and classification changes:

  • Electric vehicle passenger transport and rentals. Passenger transport and cab rental with operator, where battery charging cost is included, would have an optional 5% rate with restricted credit.
  • Delivery through e-commerce operators. Delivery services supplied by unregistered persons through an operator would be brought under Section 9(5), at 5% without credit. Courier and postal services are excluded.
  • Waste and scrap. Plastic, e-waste, tyre scrap and used cooking oil supplied by unregistered persons to registered businesses would move to reverse charge, with 2% TDS on business-to-business supplies of such waste.
  • Second-hand vehicle dealers. Dealers under the margin scheme would get credit on inputs and input services, though not on the vehicles themselves.
  • Nil rate: psyllium (isabgol) seeds in all forms. Aligned rates: retreaded tractor tyres with new tractor tyres.
  • Classification clarity: sublimation paper (heading 4809), all toys under heading 9503, and seaweed-based bio-stimulants (heading 3101), with past cases regularised where stated.
  • Exemptions for items such as warehousing of sowing seeds, coffee curing, helicopter seat-sharing in the North East, Sikkim and Bagdogra, and the toll-collection rights under the TOT model.

As always, rate changes apply only from the date of the notification. Read the notification itself for conditions and effective dates.

Checklist for the coming quarter

  • Check each product and service line against the current notification, not an old rate chart.
  • Review reverse charge exposure if you buy scrap, waste or used oil from unregistered suppliers.
  • If you sell through a marketplace, find out whether the operator now collects tax on your delivery or transport services.
  • If your output rate fell and your input rate did not, calculate accumulated credit and talk to us about refund eligibility.

  • Business Standard: GST Council adopts two-rate structure
  • Recommendations of the 57th Meeting of the GST Council (PIB)

GST Appellate Tribunal is now hearing cases: what businesses should know

After years of delay, the GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) has started hearing appeals. Here is the timeline, the filing windows and how the pre-deposit works.

By KS Financials · Updated 18 Nov 2026 · 3 min read

For years, a GST dispute that lost at the first appeal stage had nowhere to go except the High Court, because the Tribunal that the law promised had not been set up. That has changed. The GST Appellate Tribunal now has a working portal and has begun to hear matters, which makes a second appeal on facts available again.

A note on sources: the dates below come mainly from a professional firm's article and press reports, not from the Tribunal's own notifications. Check the dates against the GSTAT portal before relying on them for a deadline.

Timeline

  • 24 September 2025: GSTAT was formally launched and its e-filing portal went live.
  • 16 December 2025: filing opened for backlog appeals, meaning appeals against older orders.
  • 1 November 2025: the pre-deposit required for an appeal to the Tribunal was reduced from 20% to 10% of the disputed tax (subject to a cap).
  • 16 February 2026: hearings began at the Principal Bench and State Benches.
  • 30 June 2026: reported as the final date to file appeals against orders passed before 1 April 2026. That date has now passed. If you missed it, take advice about whether any relief is possible.
  • From 1 April 2026: for new orders, the normal time limit is three months from the date of the first appellate order.

How the appeal path works

  1. The officer issues a notice and then an order.
  2. You appeal to the first appellate authority, paying a pre-deposit of 10% of the disputed tax.
  3. If you lose, you can appeal to the GST Appellate Tribunal within the time limit, paying a further pre-deposit.
  4. Beyond the Tribunal, questions of law can go to the High Court.

The Tribunal matters because it is the last forum that decides facts. A good set of records, reconciliations and evidence prepared early often decides the outcome.

Related changes from the 57th Council meeting

  • Penalty-only orders: the pre-deposit for appeals against orders that impose only a penalty would be capped at ₹40 crore (₹20 crore CGST and ₹20 crore SGST).
  • Small notices: no show cause notice where the tax is below ₹10,000, and pending notices and appeals below that amount would be treated the same way.
  • Reduced penalty: a 5% penalty for non-fraud cases if tax and interest are paid within 30 days (Section 73) or 60 days (Section 74A) of the order. This can make paying a correct demand cheaper than fighting it.
  • Tribunal law: the GSTAT provisions would be aligned with the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026.
  • Advance rulings: reports say the Principal Bench of GSTAT has been empowered to act as the National Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling.

These Council items are recommendations and need notifications or amendments before they apply.

Should you appeal or pay?

There is no single answer, but these questions help:

  • Is the demand correct on the facts, even partly? If yes, paying that part early may reduce the penalty.
  • Is the issue a matter of interpretation that other taxpayers face too? Then a Tribunal order may help a wider group, and the pre-deposit is a reasonable cost.
  • Can you afford the pre-deposit without hurting working capital? Plan for it before the appeal deadline arrives.
  • Do you have the documents? E-way bills, delivery proof, bank entries and supplier confirmations win these cases.

Action list

  1. Make a register of all orders received in the last two years, with the order date and the appeal deadline.
  2. Calendar the three-month appeal limit for each new order the day it arrives.
  3. Keep a folder of supporting documents for each disputed item.
  4. Register on the GSTAT portal and test your login before you need it in a hurry.

If you have an order and are unsure whether to pay or appeal, speak to us. We can review the order, the deadline and the pre-deposit and suggest the cheaper route.

  • Latest GST Council meeting decisions, May 2026 update (TaxAJ)

The Income-tax Act, 2025 is in force: what has changed for taxpayers

India's income tax law was rewritten and replaced the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026. The rates look familiar, but the vocabulary, forms and some due dates are new.

By KS Financials · Updated 18 Nov 2026 · 3 min read

The Income-tax Act, 2025 came into force on 1 April 2026 and replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961. The government's aim was a shorter, plainer law. Reports describe it as keeping the existing tax structure largely intact, so for most taxpayers the change is about language, numbering and forms more than about tax rates. Even so, there are enough practical differences that every business and salaried client should know the basics.

The "tax year" replaces previous year and assessment year

The old law used two terms that confused many people, the previous year in which income was earned and the assessment year in which it was assessed. The new Act replaces both with a single tax year, running from 1 April to 31 March. Income earned in the tax year 2026-27 is taxed in that same tax year's framework. Income earned up to 31 March 2026 continues to be dealt with under the 1961 Act, so you will see both laws in use for a while, especially for notices and reassessments on older years.

A smaller statute

  • Sections fall from 819 to 536.
  • Rules fall from 511 to 333.
  • Forms fall from 399 to 190.
  • Deductions and exemptions are grouped into schedules and tables. The old Chapter VI-A deductions (sections 80A to 80VVA) are reorganised into sections 122 to 154.

Section numbers that every accountant knew by heart have changed. The old 80C or 194C will not appear in the same form, so references in your own templates and engagement letters need updating.

Tax rates and regime

Slabs and rates are broadly unchanged. The new tax regime remains the default, and a taxpayer can still opt for the old regime subject to the conditions. If you have been working with the Budget 2025 slab structure, that continues to apply.

Forms with new names

Old formNew formPurpose
Form 16Form 130TDS certificate for salary
Form 26ASForm 168Tax credit statement
Forms 15G and 15HForm 121Declaration to avoid TDS
Form 49AForms 93 and 94PAN application, now split

Return filing: due dates and revisions

  • The due date for ITR-3 and ITR-4 (business and professional income, and presumptive taxation) moves to 31 August from 31 July. ITR-1 and ITR-2 stay at 31 July.
  • A revised return can be filed up to 31 March of the following year.
  • The time limit for filing an updated return is extended to four years.
  • Digital filing and faceless assessment remain the default.

Deadlines are the kind of detail that should be confirmed against the CBDT notification and the Act each year, as dates can be extended.

TCS on foreign remittances

Tax collected at source on foreign remittances for education and medical purposes falls from 5% to 2%. Other remittances stay at the higher rate. We cover the wider TDS and TCS changes in a separate article.

What to do this year

  1. Update your templates. Engagement letters, checklists, payroll declarations and client reminders should use the new section numbers and form names.
  2. Brief your payroll team. Salary certificates are now Form 130 and employees may ask for the 15G/15H replacement, Form 121.
  3. Plan the business return calendar. If you file ITR-3 or ITR-4, the later due date helps, but audit cases and GST reconciliations still work to their own dates.
  4. Keep two sets of references. Old assessments, appeals and notices on income up to 31 March 2026 are still governed by the 1961 Act.
  5. Choose the regime deliberately. Compare old and new regimes each year with your actual deductions rather than defaulting.

Note: the figures above come from press summaries of the Act. Check section numbers, forms and deadlines against the official Act and CBDT notifications before relying on them for a filing.

  • Free Press Journal: New Income Tax Act replaces 1961 law from April 1, 2026
  • Taxscan: New Income Tax Act from 1st April 2026, key changes

TDS and TCS under the new Income-tax Act: new sections, forms and rates

TDS rates are mostly unchanged, but the section numbers, return forms and some TCS rates are new. A working guide for deductors.

By KS Financials · Updated 18 Nov 2026 · 3 min read

Anyone who deducts tax at source feels a change in the law first, because TDS touches payroll, vendor payments, rent and property deals every month. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, effective 1 April 2026, the reported approach is simplification: a cleaner structure with consolidated sections and forms, and relatively few rate changes. A Business Today explainer calls it a move towards "a cleaner, more structured TDS-TCS regime".

Please note: the figures here are drawn from published explainers and have not been checked line by line against the Act and Rules. Verify any figure before you apply it to a deduction.

New section numbers

PaymentOld sectionNew section
Salary192392
Interest (other than securities)194A393
Contractor payments194C393
TCS206C394 series

Many payment types that had their own section are now entries in a table under section 393, each with a code, for example 1002 for salary and 1022 for interest. You will see these codes in returns and in challans.

Return forms

  • Form 24Q (TDS on salary) becomes Form 138.
  • Form 26Q (TDS on non-salary payments) becomes Form 140.
  • Forms 26QB, 26QC, 26QD and 26QE are consolidated into Form 141.
  • Form 27EQ (TCS return) becomes Form 143.

Salary certificates are now Form 130, and the declaration forms 15G and 15H are merged into Form 121.

Rates and thresholds that are reported as retained

  • Interest: 10%, with a ₹10,000 threshold and higher limits in some cases.
  • Contractors: 1% for individuals and HUFs, 2% for others, with ₹30,000 per payment and ₹1 lakh a year limits.
  • Professional fees: 10%. Technical services: 2%.
  • Commission and brokerage: 2% above ₹20,000.
  • Rent: 2% for plant and machinery, 10% for land and buildings, with the ₹50,000 monthly threshold.
  • Property purchase: 1% above ₹50 lakh.
  • Purchase of goods: 0.1% where the buyer's turnover is above ₹10 crore and purchases from a seller exceed ₹50 lakh.

TCS changes

  • Foreign remittances under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme for education and medical purposes: from 5% to 2%. Other remittances: 20%.
  • Overseas tour packages: reported as 2%, down from 5% (up to ₹10 lakh) and 20% (above ₹10 lakh).
  • Alcohol: reported as moving from 1% to 2%. Tendu leaves: from 5% to 2%.
  • Motor vehicles above ₹10 lakh: 1%, unchanged.

The explainer lists the LRS rate under both "changed" and "unchanged", so confirm this one with the notification before you collect tax.

Other compliance changes

  • PAN instead of TAN for some property deals. From 1 October 2026, resident buyers and HUFs buying property from non-resident sellers can use PAN rather than a TAN for the deduction.
  • Lower or nil deduction certificates move to a fully electronic process in place of manual assessment.
  • GST-linked TDS. Separately, the 57th GST Council recommended 2% TDS on business-to-business supplies of specified waste and scrap. This is a GST matter and is not part of income tax.

A month-end checklist for deductors

  1. Map your vendor master. Add the new section and code beside each vendor category in your accounting software.
  2. Check your software version. Ask your payroll and accounting vendor whether returns can be generated in Forms 138, 140, 141 and 143.
  3. Keep the thresholds. Do not change deduction logic because of the renumbering. The rate and threshold you applied last year is usually the right one this year unless a rate was reported as changed.
  4. Update salary paperwork. Issue Form 130 to employees and collect declarations on Form 121 where relevant.
  5. Calendar due dates. TDS payment is due by the 7th of the following month and quarterly returns follow the usual cycle. Check the current notification for exact dates.
  6. Reconcile with Form 168. Ask vendors and employees to compare the new credit statement with your deductions each quarter to catch mismatches early.

If you want your deduction process reviewed against the new sections, or help with quarterly returns in the new forms, speak to our team.
